subject: English
board: KS3 English Language and Literature (school curriculum, building to AQA GCSE English Language 8700 and Edexcel GCSE English Literature 1ET0)
source: School 2026–27 Year 7 HT1 weekly schemes of work (The Explorer by Katherine Rundell, weeks 1–4: Transformation Begins; Survival and Setting; Trust, Leadership and Survival; Courage and Decision-Making) and the school's English frameworks (PETZAAL, STASS, APPS, VANCAPP, SOSCHAAMPS); Year 7 HT1 weekly assessment pack. The novel is in copyright, so lessons refer pupils to chapters of the class copy and do not reproduce it; practice extracts are teacher-written.

lessons.title: Meeting The Explorer: openings and first impressions
lessons.bigQuestion: How can one unexpected event change a person's life forever?
objectives: Read and discuss the opening chapters of The Explorer
Retrieve and infer information about the main character
Make and justify predictions using evidence
successCriteria: Retrieve four facts about the opening situation
Make an inference about Fred and explain it with evidence
Explain how the opening hooks the reader
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the Amazon rainforest; Science: survival needs (food, water, shelter)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: facing fear with trust in Allah (tawakkul); social: the value of every person in a group

keywords.def: find information stated directly in a text
work out something the writer suggests but does not state
an opening that grabs the reader's attention
the main character of a story
a sensible guess about what will happen, based on evidence

starter: Bismillah. Write one sentence about a time something unexpected changed your plans.
What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?
Name three things a person needs to survive.
What do you already know about the Amazon rainforest?

teach.heading: Retrieval and inference
bullets: Retrieval: the text tells you directly
Inference: you read between the lines
Both need evidence from the text
teach.note: Read Chapters 1–2 aloud from the class copy (pupils follow in theirs). Pause after the crash and ask for one fact and one inference. Misconception: pupils treat any sentence about the book as an inference; push for 'which words make you think that?'

left.title: Retrieval
points: The answer is on the page

right.title: Inference
points: What sort of person is he?

teach.heading: How openings hook us
bullets: Start in the middle of the action
Create questions in the reader's mind
Give us someone to care about
teach.note: Ask: 'What questions does the opening make you ask?' Collect three in the chat. Link to the big question: one event (the crash) changes everything.

teach.heading: Practise on a short extract
teach.note: Use this original extract to model, so we are not quoting the novel. Ask: what can we retrieve? What can we infer about the speaker?

quote.text: The engine coughed twice, then fell silent. Through the window, the green went on forever, and Sami realised he could no longer hear his own heartbeat over the roaring wind.

model.problem: What can we infer about Sami from the extract?
steps: Point: Sami is terrified
Evidence: he 'could no longer hear his own heartbeat over the roaring wind'
Explain: the noise overwhelms him, suggesting panic and danger
model.answer: A short inference paragraph using evidence

check.q: 'The engine coughed twice, then fell silent.' Which is an INFERENCE?
check.why: The danger is suggested, not stated. A, B and D are stated or retrieved.

practice: Retrieve two facts about the plane journey from Chapter 1.
Write one inference about Fred with a piece of evidence.
List two questions the opening makes you ask.
independent: Core: Write a PEE paragraph: What is your first impression of Fred?
Extend: Explain how the writer hooks the reader in the opening, using two pieces of evidence.
Stretch: Predict how Fred might change by the end of the novel. Justify your prediction with clues from Chapters 1–2.
exit: What is the difference between retrieval and inference?
Write one inference about the setting.
Make one prediction with a reason.
lessons.homework: Read Chapters 3–4 and record two facts and two inferences in your reading journal.
lessons.send: Support: sentence starters ('I can infer that… because…') and the audio version of the chapters. EAL: key word cards. Stretch: compare with another survival story you know.

lessons.title: Word classes with VANCAPP
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do writers choose some words and not others?
objectives: Identify the main word classes
Use precise verbs and adjectives
Explain the effect of a writer's word choice
successCriteria: Identify verbs, adverbs, nouns, conjunctions, adjectives, pronouns and prepositions
Replace vague words with precise ones
Explain why a precise verb is more effective
lessons.crossCurricular: Arabic: word types (ism, fi'l, harf); Science: precise vocabulary in explanations
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the power of words (good speech as charity)

keywords.def: an action, event or state: dash, became, is
describes a noun: dense, humid
adds detail to a verb: quickly, nervously
shows position or time: beneath, during
joins clauses: because, although

starter: Bismillah. Name the protagonist of The Explorer.
Write one inference about Chapter 3 or 4.
Which word is a verb: 'jungle', 'crept', 'green'?
Finish the sentence: 'I was frightened because…'

teach.heading: VANCAPP
teach.note: Display the VANCAPP poster. Pupils find one example of each from the class novel.

teach.heading: Precise verbs
bullets: Precise verbs show character and mood

model.problem: Improve: 'The boy went through the trees.'
steps: Find the vague verb: went
Ask: how did he move? Why?
Choose a precise verb: stumbled
Add a precise prepositional phrase: beneath the dripping branches
model.answer: The boy stumbled beneath the dripping branches.

teach.heading: Too many adjectives
bullets: One precise adjective beats three vague ones

misconception.wrong: The big, scary, dark, horrible forest
misconception.right: The hostile forest: one precise word

check.q: In 'The parrot screeched loudly above the river', which word is a preposition?
check.why: 'Above' shows position. 'Screeched' is a verb, 'loudly' an adverb, 'river' a noun.

practice: Label each word class in: 'Nervously, they waded across the brown river.'
Upgrade three vague verbs: went, said, looked.
Write a sentence with a preposition and an adverb.
independent: Core: Find seven words from Chapters 1–4, one for each VANCAPP class.
Extend: Rewrite a dull paragraph (provided) replacing six vague words with precise ones.
Stretch: Choose one verb from the novel. Explain in a paragraph why the writer chose it over a simpler synonym.
exit: What does an adverb do?
Give a precise verb instead of 'walked'.
Name the word class of 'although'.
lessons.homework: Complete the VANCAPP practice sheet and learn this week's Tier 2 words: dense, humid, concealed, hostile, tangled, isolated, survive, terrain.
lessons.send: Support: VANCAPP card with colour-coded examples. Stretch: identify determiners and modal verbs too.

lessons.title: How setting creates atmosphere
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a writer use setting to create tension and develop a story?
objectives: Explore how the Amazon rainforest is presented
Analyse how language creates atmosphere
Write a PETZAAL paragraph on setting
successCriteria: Find language that creates atmosphere
Use PETZAAL to explain the effect of a word or phrase
Offer an alternative interpretation of the same evidence
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: rainforest climate and layers; Science: ecosystems
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder and fear in the natural world, both signs of Allah's creation

keywords.def: where and when a story takes place
the mood or feeling a writer creates
language that creates a picture in the reader's mind
Point, Evidence, Technique, Zoom in, Analyse, Alternative, Link

starter: Give a precise verb for 'moved'.
What is an adjective?
Name two layers of a rainforest.
What does 'atmosphere' mean in a story?

teach.heading: Setting is more than a place
bullets: It can feel like an enemy
teach.note: Read the rainforest descriptions in Chapters 3–6 from the class copy. Pupils highlight words that make the place feel dangerous or beautiful.

head: Step
What to do
Sentence starter
rows: This is evident in the phrase '…'
Therefore, this reinforces the idea that…

quote.text: Vines hung like ropes from a ship that had sunk long ago, and somewhere in the dripping dark, something watched them pass.

model.problem: How does the writer make the setting threatening?
steps: P: The writer presents the forest as watchful and hostile.
E/T: The personification in 'something watched them' makes the forest seem alive.
Z: The vague word 'something' hides what it is, so we fear the unknown.
A: Alternatively, it could show the children's growing paranoia.
L: Therefore the setting itself becomes a source of tension.

check.q: Which phrase best creates a tense atmosphere?
check.why: Personified silence 'pressing' suggests threat. The others are plain description.

practice: Find two phrases from Chapters 3–6 that show danger.
Zoom in on one word: what does it suggest?
Write an alternative interpretation for one phrase.
independent: Core: Write one PETZAAL paragraph on how the rainforest is presented.
Extend: Write two paragraphs comparing beautiful and dangerous descriptions of the rainforest.
Stretch: Explain how the setting changes the characters' behaviour, linking to the big question.
exit: What does the Z in PETZAAL stand for?
Name one technique that creates atmosphere.
Write one alternative interpretation sentence.
lessons.homework: Read Chapters 7–8. Record three quotations describing the rainforest in your reading journal.
lessons.send: Support: PETZAAL writing frame with starters. EAL: atmosphere word bank. Stretch: compare two settings.

lessons.title: Writing a setting with STASS
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a writer make a reader feel they are standing inside a place?
objectives: Plan a setting description using STASS
Use expanded noun phrases and prepositional phrases
Write and improve a setting paragraph
successCriteria: Plan using all five STASS steps
Write expanded noun phrases with prepositional phrases
Choose details that build one dominant mood
lessons.crossCurricular: Art: composition and focal points; Geography: describing landscapes
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on creation through careful observation (tafakkur)

keywords.def: Setting/place, Time, Atmosphere, Senses, Significant objects
a noun with extra detail: the tangled, dripping vines
a phrase beginning with a preposition: beneath the canopy
weather or setting reflecting a character's feelings

starter: What does the second A in PETZAAL stand for?
Expand this noun: 'a river'.
Name a preposition.
Which sense is hardest to describe?

head: Step
Ask yourself
rows: Where are we? Select precise, significant details.
When is it? Season, light, weather.
What mood should the reader feel?
Sight, sound, smell, touch, taste, chosen selectively.
An object that hints at a deeper meaning.

teach.heading: Expanded noun phrases
bullets: the + rotting + log + beneath the canopy

steps: Add a determiner: the log
Add a precise adjective: the rotting log
Add a prepositional phrase: the rotting log beneath the canopy
Add a sensory detail: the rotting log beneath the canopy, soft as wet bread
model.answer: the rotting log beneath the canopy, soft as wet bread

teach.heading: Listing everything
bullets: Select details that build ONE mood
teach.note: Show the difference between a list and a focused description.

misconception.wrong: Describe every single thing you can see
misconception.right: Choose a few details that all build the same atmosphere

check.q: 'The broken compass lay half-buried in the mud.' Which STASS step is this?
check.why: The compass is an object that hints at deeper meaning (being lost). It isn't mainly about time or senses.

practice: Write one expanded noun phrase for each of: tree, sky, river.
Add a prepositional phrase to each.
Choose a mood and list three details that build it.
independent: Core: Write a STASS setting paragraph of the rainforest at dusk.
Extend: Include pathetic fallacy and a significant object with a hidden meaning.
Stretch: Write the same place twice: once peaceful, once threatening. Change only the details, not the place.
exit: What does STASS stand for?
Write an expanded noun phrase with a prepositional phrase.
What is pathetic fallacy?
lessons.homework: Redraft your setting paragraph, highlighting each STASS step in a different colour.
lessons.send: Support: STASS planning grid and word bank. Stretch: vary sentence openings with prepositional phrases.

lessons.unit: The Explorer: Trust, Leadership and Survival
lessons.title: Character and leadership
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes someone a good leader when everything goes wrong?
objectives: Analyse how characters are presented through actions and speech
Compare two characters
Use evidence to support a view about leadership
successCriteria: Describe a character with evidence
Explain how actions and dialogue reveal character
Compare two characters' leadership with a judgement
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: teamwork and resilience; Islamic Studies: leadership as responsibility (amanah)
lessons.smsc: Moral: the hadith 'Each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for his flock' (Sahih al-Bukhari 893, Sahih Muslim 1829)

keywords.def: how a writer presents a character
the words characters speak
a quality of a person's character
explain similarities and differences

starter: What does STASS stand for?
Name the four children in The Explorer.
Give one quality of a good leader.
What is dialogue?

teach.heading: How writers reveal character
teach.note: Use Chapters 7–10 from the class copy. Pupils find one example of each for Fred or Con.

teach.heading: Comparing leaders
teach.note: Build a comparison together using events from the chapters.

teach.heading: Writing a comparison
teach.note: Model a comparative sentence using two characters from the novel.

model.problem: Compare how two children respond to danger
steps: Point about character A with evidence
Comparative connective: whereas
Point about character B with evidence
Judgement: which is the better leader here and why
model.answer: A balanced comparative paragraph with a judgement

teach.heading: Retelling the story
bullets: Analysis explains HOW and WHY, not just WHAT

misconception.wrong: Fred goes into the forest and then he finds water
misconception.right: The writer shows Fred's courage through his decision to…, suggesting…

check.q: 'She handed the last biscuit to the youngest without a word.' What does this action suggest?
check.why: Giving away scarce food silently shows quiet generosity. The action reveals character.

practice: Find one action and one piece of dialogue that reveal a character's trait.
Write a comparative sentence using 'whereas'.
Decide: who is the best leader so far? One reason.
independent: Core: Write a PETZAAL paragraph on how one character is presented as a leader.
Extend: Compare two characters' leadership in two paragraphs.
Stretch: Argue whether leadership in the novel comes from courage or from kindness, using evidence from at least two chapters.
exit: Name two ways writers reveal character.
Give a comparative connective.
Who is the strongest leader so far, and why?
lessons.homework: Read Chapters 11–12. Note one moment where a character changes.
lessons.send: Support: character evidence grid. Stretch: compare with a leader from history or the Seerah.

lessons.unit: The Explorer: Trust, Leadership and Survival
lessons.title: Non-fiction: reading about the Amazon
lessons.bigQuestion: How does knowing real facts change how we read a story?
objectives: Retrieve and summarise information from a non-fiction text
Identify features of informative writing
Link factual knowledge to the novel
successCriteria: Retrieve key facts accurately
Write a concise summary in your own words
Explain how facts deepen understanding of the novel
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the Amazon basin; Science: biodiversity
lessons.smsc: Moral: protecting the Earth as khalifah (stewards)

keywords.def: writing about real facts and events
give the main points briefly in your own words
the variety of living things in a place
written to give facts and explain

starter: What does 'whereas' do in a sentence?
Name a fiction and a non-fiction text.
What is the largest rainforest on Earth?
What does 'summarise' mean?

teach.heading: Features of informative writing
teach.note: Show the school's Amazon information text. Pupils spot each feature.

teach.heading: Reading the facts
bullets: The Amazon covers about 5.5 million km²
It spans nine countries, most of it in Brazil
It is home to around 10% of known species on Earth
teach.note: These are widely cited figures; tell pupils they are approximate. Link to the novel: why would the children struggle to be found?

model.problem: Summarise a paragraph about Amazon river dangers in two sentences
steps: Underline the main idea in each sentence
Cross out examples and repetition
Rewrite the main ideas in your own words
Check: no opinions, no copying
model.answer: Two short sentences with only the key points

teach.heading: Copying is not summarising
bullets: Change the words, keep the meaning

misconception.wrong: Copy out the most important sentence
misconception.right: Rewrite the main ideas briefly in your own words

check.q: Which is the best summary of 'Piranhas have sharp teeth, but most species eat plants, insects and dead fish, and they rarely attack people'?
options: Despite their teeth, piranhas are rarely dangerous to humans
Piranhas have sharp teeth and eat insects and dead fish
check.why: B keeps the main idea in new words. A adds an opinion; C and D miss the main point.

practice: Retrieve three facts from the information text.
Summarise one paragraph in two sentences.
Find one technical word and define it.
independent: Core: Write a five-sentence summary of the Amazon information text.
Extend: Explain how two facts help us understand the children's situation in the novel.
Stretch: Write a short informative paragraph about one rainforest danger, using all four features of informative writing.
exit: Name two features of informative writing.
Why should a summary avoid opinions?
One fact that helps you understand the novel?
lessons.homework: Research one rainforest animal and write five facts in your own words.
lessons.send: Support: highlighted text with main ideas. Stretch: compare two sources on the Amazon.

lessons.title: Turning points and difficult decisions
lessons.bigQuestion: Do difficult circumstances reveal who we really are, or change us?
objectives: Identify a turning point in the novel
Analyse how a writer builds tension before a decision
Explain how characters have changed
successCriteria: Identify a turning point and explain why it matters
Analyse how sentence length builds tension
Explain character change with evidence from early and later chapters
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: decision-making; Islamic Studies: istikharah and seeking guidance
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: patience (sabr) and courage in hardship

keywords.def: a moment when the direction of the story changes
a feeling of suspense or worry
used to create shock or pace
how a character changes across a story

starter: What does 'summarise' mean?
Give one fact about the Amazon.
What is a turning point?
Name a time you had to make a hard decision (no details needed).

teach.heading: Turning points
bullets: After it, things cannot go back
Often a choice or a discovery
teach.note: Identify a turning point in Chapters 11–14 from the class copy. Ask: 'What changes after this moment?'

teach.heading: Sentence length and tension
bullets: Long sentences: build up, gather detail

quote.text: They crept along the ledge, fingers clutching wet stone, the river roaring somewhere far below them in the dark, and every step felt like a question nobody wanted to answer. Then the rock gave way.

teach.heading: Explaining the effect
bullets: Explain the effect on the reader

model.problem: How does the writer build tension in the extract?
steps: The long first sentence slows the pace and piles up dangers
We feel the characters' careful, fearful movement
The short final sentence 'Then the rock gave way.' is sudden
It shocks the reader, like the fall itself
model.answer: Long sentence builds; short sentence shocks

teach.heading: Change over time
bullets: Compare an early and a later moment

check.q: Why might a writer place a very short sentence after a long one?
options: To create a sudden shock or change of pace
check.why: Contrast in sentence length changes pace and creates impact.

practice: Identify a turning point and explain what changes.
Find a short sentence in the novel and explain its effect.
Describe how one character has changed since Chapter 1.
independent: Core: Write a paragraph explaining one turning point.
Extend: Analyse how the writer builds tension before an important decision, commenting on sentence length.
Stretch: Answer the big question in two paragraphs, using evidence from early and later chapters.
exit: Define turning point.
Effect of a short sentence?
One way a character has changed.
lessons.homework: Read Chapters 13–14 and write a diary entry as one character at the turning point.
lessons.send: Support: change-over-time grid. Stretch: track two characters' arcs.

lessons.title: Assessment, reflection and improvement
lessons.bigQuestion: What have I learned to do as a reader and writer this half-term?
objectives: Answer a reading question using PETZAAL
Write a STASS setting under timed conditions
Reflect on feedback and improve a response (DIRT)
successCriteria: Complete the reading and writing tasks in time
Use PETZAAL and STASS accurately
Improve one paragraph using feedback and set a target

keywords.def: Dedicated Improvement and Reflection Time
check carefully for errors
a specific next step to improve
the standards used to judge work

starter: What does PETZAAL stand for?
What does STASS stand for?
Name three VANCAPP word classes.
What is a turning point?

teach.heading: The assessment
teach.note: Use the school's Year 7 HT1 weekly assessment pack / 20-minute test on The Explorer.

teach.heading: What good looks like
bullets: Writing: one mood, precise words, varied sentences
teach.note: Show a model answer extract and mark it together.

teach.heading: DIRT: improving one paragraph
bullets: Rewrite one paragraph in purple pen

model.problem: Improve: 'The forest is scary because it is dark.'
steps: Add a precise quotation as evidence
Zoom in on one word
Add an alternative interpretation
Link back to the question

misconception.right: Target: zoom in on one word and explain its connotations

check.q: Which is the most useful target?
options: Add an alternative interpretation to every PETZAAL paragraph
check.why: It is specific and actionable. The others are too vague to act on.

practice: Complete Section A of the assessment.
Complete Section B.
Proofread for three errors.
independent: Core: Complete the assessment.
Extend: DIRT: improve one paragraph using feedback.
Stretch: Write a reflection: two strengths, one target, and how you will meet it.
exit: My strongest skill this half-term
My target
One thing I enjoyed about The Explorer
lessons.homework: Complete unfinished DIRT and continue reading the novel to the end.
lessons.send: Support: extra time and writing frames as agreed. Stretch: extended response question.
